The six steps of dealflow management, in the order the articles lay them out, are sourcing, filtering, diligence, decisions, closing, and follow-up: How VCs Source Deals in Emerging VC, How VCs Filter Dealflow in Emerging VC, Early Stage Diligence in Emerging VC, Decision-making in Emerging VC, Closing Deals in Emerging VC, and How VCs Manage Followup. Reading the titles in sequence was the useful part on its own. Dealflow is the stream of startups arriving at an investor, and I had been treating the whole thing as one activity called finding deals, when only the first sixth of it is finding anything.

The aspect I am least familiar with is filtering, and specifically the split between the first-level and the second-level filter. My honest situation is that I have inflow and no filter. I am an alum of Plug and Play, Grid110, and Material Change, so introductions reach me without much effort on my part, and until now I have handled each one ad hoc: a call, a good conversation, no decision. What I want to develop is a written screen I apply the same way every time, so that a pass is a repeatable decision rather than a mood, and so I can say no quickly and specifically without spending the relationship.

What I learned. A first-level filter is a mechanical screen against the thesis itself, on sector, geography, stage, and valuation range, and it is supposed to be cheap, because its only job is to clear obvious mismatches before they cost anyone a meeting. A second-level filter is where human judgment starts: a focused first call of about thirty minutes, then pre-diligence on market size, customer validation, scalability, and team depth. Three things changed how I will actually work. First, a pass is where you spend relationship capital rather than save it. The Decile article's example is an investor who passes on a company with customer retention under 50% and introduces the founder to a mentor who specializes in churn on the way out, which is the version of no I want to be known for. Second, the scale of it. VC Lab's investment process article puts numbers on the funnel: roughly 500 leads become 100 potential investments, then 50 meetings, 20 in-depth reviews, 10 due diligence processes, 5 term sheets, and 1 investment. Almost all of this job is saying no, so the cost of each no compounds, and Bessemer's Anti-Portfolio, the public list of great companies that firm passed on, is the counterweight: a filter tight enough never to waste a meeting is also tight enough to screen out the outlier. Third, and this is the one I did not expect, the article's closing example is a VC who realizes after twenty second-stage calls that her strongest filter is not financial at all, and that she is really testing for coachability and founder-solution fit. At pre-seed there is no revenue to analyze, so that is not a refinement of the screen, it is the screen. The same article makes the point that a thesis stated in four words turns everyone you meet into a deal scout, which lands for me specifically: if I cannot say my filter in one breath, the three alumni networks I am counting on cannot route deals to me.

Since writing that I built the filter and ran it, and then I ran it a second time on a cohort I had not seen when I wrote it. I screened all 40 published companies from my own accelerator's four Seattle batches against four questions: is it AI, does it touch trust between people, is it pre-seed, is it in the United States. One company out of 40 survived to diligence, and the eleven companies in the batch announced on 21 September 2026 produced none. The exercise taught me something the articles did not. The first-level filter was easy and fast, exactly as described, but almost every hard call was a company that passed all four questions and still did not belong, which is a second-level problem the articles frame as being about founder quality and traction. For me it turned out to be about the thesis itself not being precise enough to reject a near miss, so I had to write down what looks like a fit and is not before the filter would work at all.

Later in the program I want to go deeper on two of the six steps. Decisions, because I want to know how conviction actually gets formed and written down at pre-seed, when the underwriting is almost entirely the founder. And follow-up, which I suspect is the step that separates angels who see the next deal from angels who see one deal. Closing mechanics matter less to me right now, because as an angel writing personal checks I am not negotiating complicated terms yet, but I do live or die on whether founders come back.

Sources I used:

1. https://decilegroup.com/articles/deals-filtering-emerging-vc - first- and second-level filters
2. https://decilegroup.com/articles/deals-sourcing-emerging-vc - where deals actually come from
3. https://govclab.com/2023/06/14/vc-investment-process/ - the 500-to-1 funnel, step by step
4. https://www.bvp.com/anti-portfolio - the cost of a filter that is too tight

My niche is AI that rebuilds human trust: technology that builds bridges, strengthens community bonds, and fosters belonging, backed at pre-seed in the United States. Five companies from that niche that reached a notable exit or a late-stage round:

- Nextdoor, 2021, about $4.3 billion at the peak and well under $1 billion today. A private social network organized by physical neighborhood, built so that people who live near each other can actually reach each other; it went public in November 2021 by merging with Khosla Ventures Acquisition Co. II, and it has since traded down to the mid-$2s against a $10 offer price. I am writing the second half of that sentence because a 2021 valuation is a price on one day, not a standing fact, and this is the company on my own list that proves it.
- Discord, 2021, about $15 billion. Persistent voice and text communities where groups of people who would otherwise never meet build durable social ties; it reached that valuation in a $500 million round led by Dragoneer in September 2021.
- Patreon, 2021, about $4 billion. A direct membership relationship between creators and the people who value their work, in place of algorithmic distribution; it reached that valuation in a $155 million round led by Tiger Global in April 2021.
- Hive, 2021, about $2 billion. AI content moderation and understanding, sold as an API to the platforms that have to keep abuse, fraud, and synthetic media off their services; it reached that valuation in an $85 million Series D led by Glynn Capital in April 2021.
- Sift, 2021, just over $1 billion. A digital trust and safety platform that uses machine learning to tell real customers apart from fraud without adding friction for the real ones; it raised $50 million led by Insight Partners in April 2021.

Is there enough venture scale in this niche, or do I need to widen it? There is, and the honest answer changed when I re-checked my own list rather than re-reading it. All five of those marks are from 2021, and if I run a five-year window from today it starts in October 2021, which puts four of the five outside it altogether and leaves Nextdoor inside by about four weeks. Nextdoor has given its number back. Discord has been marked down from $15 billion on the secondary market. So if the case for scale in my niche rests on that list, it rests on the top of a cycle, and I would be arguing for my own thesis with prices that no longer exist.

It does not have to rest there. When I ran the same question across the last five years instead of 2021, what came back is AI-native, American, and passes the test I apply, which is whether a product changes how two people regard each other or only how one party regards a machine. OpenEvidence raised $250 million in January 2026 at a $12 billion valuation, co-led by Thrive and DST, and what it does is hand a clinician cited medical evidence at the point of care, so the citation is a receipt a patient or a second opinion can actually check. Abridge raised $300 million in June 2025 at $5.3 billion, led by Andreessen Horowitz, turning the doctor and patient conversation into the clinical note, which gives back the thing that was being lost: the clinician's attention on the person instead of on a screen. Persona raised $200 million in April 2025 at $2 billion, co-led by Founders Fund and Ribbit, and it verifies that whoever is on the other end of an interaction is a real and specific human, which on an internet filling with software agents is the precondition for two strangers trusting each other at all. Hippocratic AI raised $126 million in November 2025 at $3.5 billion, led by Avenir Growth, with patient-facing AI that reaches out between visits, and I am listing it with an argument attached rather than as a clean fit, because an AI that calls a patient instead of a nurse calling them might be standing in for a human relationship rather than strengthening one. That is a question my own anti-thesis has to answer and has not answered yet.

So there is venture scale in this niche, and the live examples are more recent and larger than the ones I started with. Two things in that finding are uncomfortable and I would rather write them down than round them off. The first is that the newest and largest examples are not community products. The language in my thesis is bridges, community bonds, and belonging, and the companies that reached real scale by changing how two people regard each other mostly did it between a patient and a clinician. The second is that the direction of travel runs against the list I started with: the 2021 community cohort is the group that de-rated, and the AI-native group is the one that went up, most of it in the last eighteen months. I am not going to resolve that by quietly rewriting my thesis to say healthcare, because a five-year backward-looking window tells me where outcomes landed and not where the next ones will come from. But the gap between what my thesis says and what its own test returns is real, it is the most interesting thing in my notebook right now, and I would rather submit it as an open question I am carrying than as one I have closed.

I should also be straight about a tension inside the original five. The test I now apply is whether a product changes how two people regard each other or only how one party regards a machine, and fraud scoring sold to a platform is closer to the second. I am keeping Hive and Sift on the list as evidence that AI-native trust infrastructure does reach venture scale, while being clear that they sit on the boundary of my niche rather than at the center of it.

That boundary is worth pricing, because there is a version of this answer that clears ten companies without an argument and I do not think I am entitled to it. If I let identity infrastructure count as my niche, the names are there and the numbers are large. Socure raised $450 million at a $4.5 billion valuation in November 2021, led by Accel and T. Rowe Price. Alloy raised $100 million at $1.35 billion in September 2021, led by Lightspeed, and added a $52 million extension the following year at $1.55 billion. Both decide whether a person presenting themselves to a bank or a platform is who they claim to be, and counting them would take my list past ten in one move. I am not going to count them, for two reasons. The first is what is actually being decided: the platform gets a score and the person being verified gets nothing they can hold, which is the exact move my own first exclusion exists to prevent, and if I make it here then every company I rejected for protecting a machine rather than a relationship walks back in through the door I just opened. The second reason is the one that settles it. Both of those marks are from 2021, so widening the niche does not even fix the problem I started this answer with. I would be buying ten companies at the price of a definition I do not hold and a set of 2021 prices I had just finished distrusting.

So here is the test I set myself in August, run honestly: name ten United States companies from the last five years that fit this thesis and reached a billion dollars. On my own definition the count is six. Nextdoor, Discord, Patreon, Hive, Sift, and Abridge, with OpenEvidence, Persona and Hippocratic AI arguable in either direction depending on how hard I push the line. Six is not ten, and I would rather submit the number I got than the number I was hoping for. What it tells me is narrower and more useful than what I wrote the test to find out. The constraint is not the size of the outcomes, which I come back to below. It is the density: the outcomes in this niche are large and there are not many of them yet. Thin is survivable for the angel checks I am writing now, where I need one good company at a time and not a portfolio shape. Thin is a problem for a fund I would try to raise in 2026, because six companies in five years is not enough to build a portfolio around, and that is the first thing an LP would ask me. That is the angel-first, fund-later order I had already chosen, with a number attached to it for the first time, and the number is the reason the order is right rather than just my preference. The call I would most expect to be argued with is Persona, which I keep because telling a human from a software agent is a question about two people and not about a machine, and I would rather name that as the line I have to defend than leave it sitting there unmarked.

I then tested the same question from the other end, on live companies rather than on exits, and then I got to run the test again on a cohort I had never seen. I screened all 40 published companies from my own accelerator's four Seattle batches against my thesis. Thirty-seven were a clear no, one is worth a conversation but is past my entry point at a $5 million seed, one is in diligence, and one is a near miss I will come back to. The second screen is the more useful of the two, because I did not pick the companies and I already had the filter written down before I saw them. The batch announced on 21 September 2026 has eleven companies in it, ten of them in Seattle. Zero of the eleven are a clean fit. Six of the eleven are life sciences, which is the single category my own exclusion about AI as a method rather than as the substance was written to reject, so the filter did exactly what it was built to do and I cannot complain about the result. One of the eleven is the near miss and it is worth more to me than the nine easy rejections. Athanor AI produces a mathematical proof that AI-generated chip-design code does what it claims, which a third party can check without trusting the vendor. That is structurally the same product as the one company I have in diligence. I screened Athanor out, because the proof is handed to a chip designer rather than to a person the system acts upon, and I kept the other one, because its receipt is meant for an auditor or a patient. That is a real distinction and it is also a narrow one, and I would rather submit it as the place my thesis is thinnest than pretend the call was obvious. A one-in-forty hit rate against my own warmest source of dealflow is a real number and it cuts both ways. It tells me the filter works, because it rejected thirty-seven companies specifically rather than vaguely. It also tells me something I did not want to learn, which is that two consecutive cohorts of the accelerator I keep naming as my edge have produced one company I would write a check into. The reading I take from that is not that the thesis should widen. It is that this accelerator is a general-purpose regional program with heavy life-sciences weighting, and it is the wrong instrument for a filter this narrow. I have been treating it as my primary channel because I am an alum, which is a fact about my history rather than about where my deals are. If I want to write ten angel checks in this niche I need roughly ten sources, or I need to be sourcing before companies reach an accelerator at all, which is what my alumni relationships are actually for.

What I am not going to do is widen the niche. As an angel writing personal checks I do not need a decacorn for the math to work, and the evidence above says this niche produces outcomes at every size I care about. It does change the answer to the open question I had already written down, which is whether a trust and belonging filter selects for or against outlier outcomes. In August my honest read was that it selects for a slower shape of outcome, because the AI-native examples I had topped out between $1 and $4 billion. That read was wrong, and it was wrong because I was looking at a 2021 cohort: OpenEvidence went from roughly $6 billion in October 2025 to $12 billion in January 2026. The ceiling I was worried about was a ceiling on one vintage, not on the thesis. What I still do not know, and will not learn from valuations, is whether this filter selects for outcomes I can actually get access to at pre-seed. That is a different question and it is the one that binds me.

The earliest backers of each, and how those relationships likely formed:

- Nextdoor: Shasta Ventures, seed, October 2011, before the neighborhood-by-neighborhood growth pattern was visible. Benchmark, with Bill Gurley leading, in the $18.6 million round announced July 2012 alongside Greylock Partners and DAG Ventures. The relationship almost certainly predates the company: Nirav Tolia was a repeat founder who had co-founded Epinions, so the seed investors were people who had watched him work before there was anything to evaluate.
- Discord: YouWeb's 9+ incubator at the seed stage, into Hammer and Chisel, the game studio that became Discord. Then Mitch Lasky at Benchmark, who led an $8.2 million round in November 2013, before Discord existed as a product, with Accel and Tencent also in early. Jason Citron had already built and sold OpenFeint to GREE for $104 million in 2011, and Lasky had backed Riot Games, so this was a repeat-founder bet made by investors who knew the category and the person.
- Patreon: a $2.1 million seed in August 2013, co-led by Freestyle Capital and Index Ventures, with Alexis Ohanian among the angels. Jack Conte was a working musician with an audience before he was a founder, which means the problem he was solving was one he could describe from the inside. That is founder-market fit an investor can verify in a single conversation.
- Hive: General Catalyst and 8VC among the earliest institutional backers, with the company starting as a consumer app and pivoting at the end of 2017 to sell the content moderation tooling it had built for itself. The money predates the business that made the company, which is worth noticing: those investors backed a team through a pivot into an entirely different product.
- Sift: Y Combinator, Summer 2011 batch, then a Series A led by Union Square Ventures with Albert Wenger joining the board, and First Round Capital and Max Levchin in early alongside. This is the cleanest accelerator-to-institutional path of the five. The founders were ex-Google engineers, YC was the entry point, and the early institutional investors were people the accelerator put in the room.

What that pattern tells me. Four of the five earliest relationships came from somebody having watched the founder work before there was a company to evaluate: a prior startup, a prior audience, a prior batch. Only one came from a formal program, and even that one worked because the program put the founders in front of investors who would not otherwise have met them. That is exactly the mechanism my own edge runs on, and it is an argument for staying visible inside Plug and Play, Grid110, and Material Change between programs rather than only during them. I got a live confirmation of that in the screen above. The strongest company to come out of it, Glacis, took its first money from the AI2 Incubator and from Geoff Ralston's Safe Artificial Intelligence Fund. That is the same incubator-to-institutional path Sift took, running right now, inside one of my own three ecosystems.

[YOUR PARAGRAPH - OUTREACH. This is the set's last clause and it is the one thing here I cannot write for you. Contact at least three sources from the research above, then replace this bracket with a couple of sentences on who you contacted, what you said, and any initial responses. No response yet is a real answer inside a one-week window, and the sprint guidance says so outright. Warmest realistic targets, in order, and all three now have a specific reason to write rather than a generic one: whoever runs Plug and Play Seattle, because you have now screened all four of their published batches and because their Batch 4 investor expo is on 3 December at the Boeing Future of Flight in Mukilteo, which is a reason to be in the room rather than a favour to ask; the Glacis founder, which doubles as Set 4's interview and is the single message that unblocks the most work in this submission; and Miki Reynolds at Grid110, because their public founder directory stops at Cohort 25 and the current roster is not reachable from outside, which makes one message the cheapest possible test of whether the alumni edge in your thesis is an asset or a story.]

I ran three different sourcing channels this sprint rather than waiting for introductions to arrive, found a fourth while writing the memo in the set below, and comparing them against each other turned out to be the useful part of the exercise. My honest situation going into the sprint was inflow without a filter, so the first thing I did was point a filter at a list I could actually enumerate.

Channel one was my own accelerator. I screened every company Plug and Play Seattle has published across its first four batches, 40 in all, against the thesis, which is AI that rebuilds human trust, at pre-seed, in the United States. Plug and Play is one of the three ecosystems I came up through, so this was my claimed dealflow edge tested against a real list rather than asserted on a slide. I wrote a one-line decision note for every one of the 40, including the passes, because a pass with a stated reason is data about my filter and a pass without one is not. Thirty-seven were passes, one is worth tracking, one is a near miss, and one went into diligence.

The fourth batch is the part of this worth reading, because it is the only one I screened without having picked the companies and with the filter already written down. Plug and Play Seattle announced it on 21 September 2026: eleven companies, ten of them in Seattle, a twelve-week program running now, and an investor and corporate-partner expo on 3 December at the Boeing Future of Flight in Mukilteo. Zero of the eleven are a clean fit. Six are life sciences, which is the exact category my exclusion about AI as a method rather than as the substance exists to reject. One, Athanor AI, is a genuine near miss: it produces a mathematical proof that AI-generated chip-design code does what it claims, which a third party can verify without trusting the vendor, and that is structurally the same product as the company I have in diligence. I screened it out because the proof is handed to a chip designer rather than to someone the system acts upon, and I want to be honest that the gap between those two calls is one sentence wide. A second, Coda AI, pairs a language model with deterministic computation so a vehicle diagnosis can be checked rather than taken on faith, and a mechanic and a car owner is one of the genuinely low-trust exchanges in ordinary life. I have it out on the efficiency exclusion, because the sale is made on diagnostic accuracy and shop throughput, and that is the call on this list I would most happily be argued out of.

The passes did more work than the hit did. Writing thirty-seven reasons in a row made me name the four ways a company can look like this thesis and not be it: trust in machines rather than trust between people, AI as a method rather than as the substance, efficiency dressed up as connection, and AI that spends trust rather than building it. That last group is the one that proves the filter works, because those companies are AI, United States, pre-seed and human-facing, and still wrong. The test I came out of the screen with is one line, and I now apply it before anything else: does this change how two people regard each other, or only how one party regards a machine?

Channel two is public securities filings, and it is the one that changed how I think about sourcing. Any company raising on a Regulation D exemption has to file a Form D with the SEC within 15 days of first sale, and that filing states the size of the offering, how much has already been sold, and the names of the officers and directors. It is a public list of companies that are provably raising right now, and nobody has to tell me anything for me to read it. So I ran it: SEC EDGAR full-text search, form type D, Washington State business address, filed between 4 June and 2 September 2026. That returned 873 filings. Removing funds, SPVs, limited partnerships and real-estate vehicles by entity name left 71 operating companies. Keeping only those offering six million dollars or less with capital actually sold left 39. I then pulled each filing's own XML for the offering size, the amount sold, the amount still open, the year of incorporation, and the named officers, which narrowed it to nine companies incorporated in 2023 or later with a round still open and a founder named.

Channel three is the one I have not been able to run on my own, and I would rather say that than describe it as done. It is asking my own alumni networks directly, Grid110's current cohort and Material Change's portfolio and alumni, where founders are by definition raising or about to be. There is a specific finding inside that gap and it is not flattering to me. Grid110's public founder directory stops at Cohort 25, and no current roster is published anywhere reachable from outside the program, so the only way to see who is raising there right now is to ask someone inside it. That is precisely what my thesis means when it claims an alumni edge. It also means one unsent message is the entire difference between the edge being an asset and the edge being a story, and as of today the message is unsent. [BEFORE SUBMITTING - THE ECOSYSTEM CHANNEL. Write one or two sentences here on who you actually asked and what came back, or state plainly that this channel has not been run yet. Do not let it read as though it has.]

Channel four I did not plan and would not have found except by writing the deal memo in the set below, which is the reason I am reporting it here rather than saving it. The company I have in diligence publishes its receipt format as an open standard and runs the registry of systems that implement it, and in September 2026 it announced that two outside bodies, the Coalition for Health AI and the AIGovOps Foundation, will take over stewardship of that standard with the company staying on as a non-voting editor. A registry of companies that have chosen to make their AI's behaviour verifiable to the people it affects is a self-selecting list of my thesis, assembled by somebody else, maintained for reasons that have nothing to do with me. I have not sourced a single company from it yet and I am not going to claim otherwise, so I am listing it as a channel I have identified and not yet run. What makes it worth more than the other three to me is that none of the other three are specific to my thesis: an accelerator list is everyone in a city, a Form D screen is everyone who filed, and an alumni network is everyone I happen to know. This is the first channel I have found whose selection criterion is the thesis itself, and I only know it exists because I did the diligence.

A Form D says that a company is raising and who signed the filing. It does not say what the company does, so those nine were candidates and not pipeline until I went and found out. I researched each one from company sites, press, and public professional profiles, and then ran each through the one-line test above. Seven of the nine I could identify well enough to have an opinion about. Here is where they landed, because the rejections are the part that shows the filter working.

One is a real candidate, and the way I got it wrong first is the most useful thing in this set. Senior Year, Inc., in Bellevue, incorporated 2024, with Diane Lansinger named on the filing as its executive officer. From the filing alone I had written it down as a texting product that keeps older adults and the people who love them in regular contact, and I had it as the one company on the list that passed my thesis without an argument. Then I found the product. It trades as CozyText, at cozytext.com, and the company's own headline is "Know they're safe with CozyText": a text every morning with a different question, the person's answer passed on to a Trusted Circle of family or a senior community, and an alert to that circle when no answer comes. That is a more interesting company than the one I had written down, and a harder call. The case for it under my thesis is in the details rather than the pitch. The check-in asks a question instead of reading a sensor, the older person answers in their own words, and the product then asks whether there is anything they want passed on, which keeps them a participant with something to say rather than a status light on somebody else's dashboard. The case against it is the headline. What the adult child is buying is peace of mind, and peace of mind is risk reduction, which sits close to the exclusion in my own anti-thesis that says a company whose outcome metric is time or cost saved is an efficiency company rather than a trust company, and worry saved is that same metric in a warmer coat. Where I land is that it stays in the pipeline as the strongest candidate I have outside the one company already in diligence, and that the question which decides it is one to ask the founder rather than answer from a desk: does a family use this to stay in touch, or to avoid having to?

Four are out, and what makes that useful is that they are out for reasons I had already written down rather than reasons I invented to fit. Kumio, in Seattle, builds agentic cybersecurity for AI data centres. The founders are genuinely impressive and the product protects the machine, so no human relationship changes by it existing, which is the same shape I rejected once already in the accelerator screen. Opgate, in Richland, reads from its founders' own public description as runtime security for AI agents, which puts it in the same category, though I want to flag that I could not confirm the product behind that filing and I am not treating a same-name website as evidence. Tursio, in Sammamish, does enterprise search and generative AI over existing databases, which is AI as method rather than substance, and it fails on stage before it fails on thesis, with $1.47M already raised and institutional investors on the cap table. Civarro, in Kirkland, is data centre energy management and still in stealth, which is infrastructure where the receipt never lands in a human's hands.

Two I was not deciding from a desk, and re-checking their filings before submitting decided one of them for me, which is itself the argument for using this channel on a clock rather than once. MedServ Marketplace, in Sammamish, matches biomedical equipment technicians and field service engineers to hospitals and manufacturers. It is human-to-human by construction, and the outcome a buyer judges it on is equipment uptime, which is the efficiency exclusion. My read is that it matches labour rather than building a bond, so it is out on thesis, but the argument is closer than the verdict suggests. Re-pulling its filings today changed my read of it more than anything else in this set, and it is the one piece of this answer I would not have got from a single pass. MedServ has filed three separate Form Ds in five months, all of them new notices rather than amendments to one offering, and the sequence runs in the wrong direction: filed 3 March 2026, $1,000,000 offered with $275,000 sold; filed 25 June, $250,000 offered with $75,000 sold; filed 27 July, $200,000 offered with $5,000 sold and $195,000 still open on a first sale of 24 July. Each round is smaller than the one before it and each one has sold less. I do not know what that means and I am not going to guess from a filing, because a company can restructure a raise for good reasons. What I do know is that it is the opposite shape of the company I had written down last week as still live and merely smaller than I thought, and that a founder should be asked about it directly rather than have it inferred. NAMSOFT, trading as Plutus, in Kirkland, lets retail investors mirror a thematic portfolio from an independent research provider into their own brokerage account. That is a trust intermediary between a person and a stranger whose judgment they are choosing to follow, which was nearer my thesis than anything on the list except Senior Year, and what made me hesitate was that the trust runs one way and is priced, which reads more like a marketplace for reputation than a bond between people. I no longer have to settle that, because the company settled it: an amended filing on 14 September 2026 shows a $3,800,000 offering fully sold with nothing remaining. It is not a pre-seed company raising, it is a company that closed a round roughly four times the size of the one I screened, and it is out on stage rather than on thesis. The lesson I am taking from that is about the channel rather than the company. A Form D is a snapshot with no expiry date printed on it, and a screen I ran in one afternoon decays quietly while I am still citing it, so re-probing the filings is part of the method now and not a tidying step.

Two I still cannot screen, and after doing the work they are unscreened for two different reasons. Adaptive Logic, in Olympia, has no site, no press, and no public profile I could match to the filing, so it is unidentified rather than rejected, and those are different things. Vellora, in Seattle, I went and researched properly, and the finding is that there is nothing public to find: incorporated in 2026, $1.3 million offered with $1,222,000 still open as of its filing, one person named on it, a first sale in August, and no product, no site, and no press anywhere I could reach. If that person is the Bryan Copley who founded CityBldr here in Seattle, and the name and the city match although I have not confirmed it is the same person, then this is a repeat local founder raising quietly. That is exactly the company an alumni network can introduce me to and a public database cannot, and it is the clearest argument I have for why channel three is not optional.

What the comparison actually taught me is the honest finding of this sprint. The public filings channel produced nine live, dated, verifiable candidates in an afternoon and zero warmth: I know exactly how much each company is raising and how much is left, and I have no reason for any of them to take my call. My key learnings from the first half of the program. The one that reorganized how I read a cap table is that being early does not mean being paid first: proceeds run through a distribution waterfall in a strict order, capital back first, then a preferred return of around 8%, then carry, and among preferred shareholders the later rounds are usually paid before the earlier ones. When Kabbage sold, Series F took $161 million, then Series E took $166 million, then D took $50 million, then C took $31 million, leaving $22 million for Series A and B while common shareholders still held roughly 28% of the company. The second is structural: what looks like one venture firm is three entities, a management company, a fund and a general partner, doing deliberately separated jobs, and the separation is the discipline rather than the paperwork. The third is about my own position, and it is the one that changed what I do rather than what I know. I came into this program planning to learn how to run a fund, and I am leaving the first half convinced that the order matters more than the destination, which means angel checks first, then a real track record, then a fund. The fourth I learned by doing rather than by reading: a thesis is only a filter once you run it against a list you did not pick. Screening 40 companies across four accelerator batches produced 37 passes, and it was the passes, not the one hit, that showed me where the edge of my own thesis actually sits. The second half of that lesson arrived later and cost me something. One in forty, against the accelerator I had been naming as my edge, is the filter working and the channel failing at the same time, and I had been reading it as access rather than as instrument choice. The sharpest version of that came when I turned the finished filter on my own earlier work. In July I wrote five wedge statements and declared one of them ready, an AI operations partner for teams under ten people, and all five are efficiency plays: hours reclaimed, ramp time saved, a salary deferred. My anti-thesis now says that if the outcome metric in the pitch is time or cost saved, it is an efficiency company, and efficiency is orthogonal to trust. My July wedge fails my August filter, and I would rather report that than quietly restate it, because a thesis that cannot say no to my own prior work will not say no to a founder's pitch either.
